name: Clonidine (Kapvay, Catapres)
summary: Nonstimulant alpha-2 agonist used in psychiatry for ADHD, tics, PTSD-related hyperarousal, and sleep problems—originally an antihypertensive, so blood pressure and heart rate must be monitored and it should never be stopped abruptly.
description: Clonidine is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist originally developed to treat high blood pressure. In psychiatry, extended-release clonidine (Kapvay, Onyda XR) is used as a nonstimulant option for ADHD, especially when hyperactivity, impulsivity, tics, aggression, or sleep problems are prominent. Immediate-release clonidine is also used off-label for PTSD-related hyperarousal and nightmares, opioid withdrawal symptoms, and insomnia in people with neurodevelopmental disorders. Because clonidine lowers blood pressure and slows heart rate, dosing must be careful and gradual, and it should never be stopped suddenly due to risk of rebound hypertension.
patient_summary: Clonidine is a blood pressure medicine that psychiatrists also use to help with ADHD, tics, PTSD symptoms (like being on edge or having nightmares), and sleep. It tends to calm the body more than the mind: people often feel less restless, less "amped up," and sleepier. Because it lowers blood pressure and heart rate, it can make you dizzy or lightheaded, especially when you stand up quickly. You should not stop clonidine suddenly—this can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure. Your dose needs to be adjusted slowly with your prescriber and your blood pressure and pulse should be checked regularly.

metadata.pharmacologic_category: Alpha2-Adrenergic Agonist; Antihypertensive; Nonstimulant ADHD Medication

primary_indications: ADHD with comorbid tics or Tourette syndrome
ADHD with sleep-onset insomnia or evening hyperactivity

linked_conditions.context: Extended-release clonidine (Kapvay, Onyda XR) is FDA-approved for ADHD in children ≥6 as monotherapy or adjunct to stimulants. Particularly helpful for hyperactivity, impulsivity, aggression, tics, and sleep onset problems.
Used off-label to reduce motor and vocal tics, especially in youth with comorbid ADHD. Often preferred over antipsychotics when tics are moderate and attention/sleep symptoms are present.
Immediate-release clonidine is sometimes used off-label to reduce hyperarousal, startle, irritability, and sleep disruption in PTSD, especially when nightmares and autonomic symptoms are prominent.
Commonly used in children and teens with ADHD or autism-related insomnia to help with sleep initiation. Not a first-line sleep medication in adults without neurodevelopmental conditions.
Used as an adjunct or alternative to opioid agonist therapy to reduce withdrawal-related sweating, agitation, restlessness, and elevated heart rate/blood pressure in supervised settings.

Originally approved for chronic high blood pressure. In modern practice, not usually first-line but may be used when other agents are insufficient or not tolerated. Psychiatric prescribers must remember all psych doses still act as an antihypertensive.

contraindications: Known hypersensitivity to clonidine or any component of the formulation
Acute severe bradyarrhythmia, second- or third-degree AV block, or sick sinus syndrome (particularly without a pacemaker)
Significant symptomatic hypotension or episodes of syncope related to low blood pressure
Severe cerebrovascular disease where abrupt blood pressure changes could be dangerous
Use of epidural clonidine in patients with infection at the injection site, bleeding diathesis, or anticoagulant therapy
Abrupt discontinuation after chronic use (functional contraindication due to rebound hypertension risk)

efficacy_response.comparison_data: Most trials show clinically meaningful reductions in hyperactivity, impulsivity, and oppositional behavior, with smaller effects on core inattention. Best evidence is in children and adolescents with ADHD, especially when tics, aggression, or insomnia are also present.
efficacy_response.patient_text: Studies suggest clonidine helps many children with ADHD feel less restless, less impulsive, and sleep more reliably. It tends to calm the body more than sharpen attention, so it is often combined with a stimulant if focus is still a major problem.
efficacy_response.citation_tag: Psychiatric use supported by randomized trials in pediatric ADHD and tic disorders; no single landmark trial defines a simple percentage like with some stimulant studies.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Well absorbed orally. Immediate-release tablets reach peak blood levels in ~1 to 3 hours. Extended-release forms (Kapvay, Onyda XR, Nexiclon XR) have slower absorption with peak around 7 to 8 hours.
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: ~70–80% for immediate-release; extended-release and suspension have similar overall exposure but different time profiles.
pharmacokinetics.onset: For sedation and blood pressure effects, 30–60 minutes (oral IR). ADHD symptom improvement typically emerges over 1–2 weeks on a stable extended-release dose.
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: 1–3 hours (IR), ~7–8 hours (ER tablets and XR suspension).
pharmacokinetics.half_life: Adults with normal kidney function: ~12–16 hours; prolonged up to ~41 hours in severe renal impairment.
pharmacokinetics.duration_IR: Most of the clinical sedative and blood pressure effect lasts ~6–10 hours; often dosed 2–4 times daily in off-label use.
pharmacokinetics.duration_ER: Extended-release preparations provide ~24-hour coverage with once- or twice-daily dosing depending on the product.
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Hepatic metabolism to inactive metabolites; also undergoes enterohepatic recirculation.
pharmacokinetics.excretion: 40–60% eliminated in urine as unchanged drug; remainder as metabolites.
pharmacokinetics.food_effect: Food does not meaningfully change overall absorption, but taking it consistently with or without food helps keep levels steady.

sections.heading: What It's Used For (Psychiatry-Focused)
sections.text: Clonidine started out as a blood pressure medication, but psychiatrists now use it widely for ADHD and related conditions, especially when hyperactivity, impulsivity, tics, aggression, or sleep problems are a concern.
items: {link:condition:attention-deficit-hyperactivity-disorder:ADHD in children and teens}: FDA-approved extended-release clonidine (Kapvay, Onyda XR) can be used alone or with stimulants, particularly when hyperactivity and behavioral dysregulation are prominent.
ADHD with tics or Tourette syndrome: Often chosen when stimulants worsen tics or when tics and hyperactivity co-occur.
ADHD with severe bedtime restlessness or insomnia: Evening clonidine can help kids and teens settle and fall asleep more easily.
{link:condition:posttraumatic-stress-disorder:PTSD-related hyperarousal}: Off-label use to reduce being “on edge,” startle responses, and sleep disruption, sometimes alongside prazosin or SSRIs.
Opioid withdrawal (medically supervised): Off-label, used to reduce sweating, agitation, and elevated pulse and blood pressure during detox.
Insomnia in neurodevelopmental disorders: Often used in autism or intellectual disability when behavioral interventions alone are not enough.
Primary hypertension: Still used by some clinicians for chronic high blood pressure. All psychiatric prescribers must remember that clonidine always has cardiovascular effects, even at “psych doses.”
off_label: Tourette syndrome and chronic tic disorders
Aggression/irritability in disruptive behavior disorders (as adjunct)
Sleep disturbance in ADHD or autism spectrum disorder
Transition off ICU sedative dexmedetomidine to oral therapy

sections.heading: What People Typically Notice
sections.intro: Experiences vary, but these are common patterns people describe when taking clonidine for mental health reasons:

quotes: My body finally felt like it could sit still.
The constant motor in my son’s legs quieted down.
I wasn’t so jumpy or ‘wired’ all evening.
It made me pretty sleepy at first, especially at night.
I could fall asleep much faster, but I also felt groggy in the morning.
If I took it too early in the day, I just wanted to nap.
items.note: Sedation is very common, especially when first starting or increasing the dose.

quotes: If I stood up too fast, I got lightheaded.
My heart didn’t pound as much when I was anxious.
I learned to get out of bed slowly so I didn’t feel faint.
items.note: Because clonidine lowers blood pressure and heart rate, dizziness on standing is a key side effect to watch for.

quotes: I was still distractible, but way less hyper.
Her tics were less frequent and less intense.
It didn’t sharpen my focus like a stimulant, but it kept me from bouncing off the walls.
When I forgot a dose, my heart raced and I felt awful.
Stopping suddenly made my blood pressure shoot up.
I learned the hard way that you can’t just quit it overnight.
items.note: Never stop clonidine abruptly—rebound high blood pressure and withdrawal symptoms can be serious.

sections.heading: How Fast It Works & How Long It Lasts
sections.text: Clonidine is not an instant "focus" pill like some stimulants, but some effects are felt quickly while others build over weeks.
key_points: 30–60 minutes: Onset of calming and blood pressure–lowering effects with immediate-release tablets.
1–3 hours: Peak effect for IR tablets (most sedation and blood pressure effect).
6–10 hours: Typical duration of a single immediate-release dose, which is why off-label psychiatric uses often require 2–4 daily doses.
7–8 hours: Time to peak for extended-release clonidine (Kapvay, Onyda XR, Nexiclon XR), with smoother all-day coverage.
1–2 weeks: Usual time frame to see meaningful ADHD symptom improvement once a consistent dose is reached.
2–3 days: Time for transdermal patches to reach steady levels after application.
12–16 hours: Average time for half of the drug to leave the body in adults with normal kidney function.

sections.heading: How Well It Works in Psychiatry
sections.comparison: Less potent than stimulants for attention, but valuable for hyperactivity, impulsivity, tics, and sleep.
sections.text: In ADHD, clonidine is not usually as powerful as stimulants for improving pure inattention, but it can substantially reduce hyperactivity, impulsivity, aggression, and difficulty winding down at night. It is especially useful in children who have tics, marked irritability, or cannot tolerate higher stimulant doses because of side effects. In PTSD, small studies and clinical experience support benefits in reducing hyperarousal and improving sleep, though it is considered an adjunct rather than a primary treatment.
sections.clinical_details: In pediatric ADHD trials, extended-release clonidine has shown statistically significant improvements in ADHD rating scales versus placebo, particularly on hyperactivity/impulsivity and oppositional behavior. Benefits in sleep onset latency have also been observed. In tic disorders, clonidine provides modest symptom reductions and is often best when combined with behavioral therapy or stimulants. For PTSD and insomnia, evidence is more limited and largely based on smaller studies and clinical practice.

citation.authors: Multiple randomized controlled trials and clinical guidelines
citation.title: Alpha-2 agonists in the treatment of ADHD and related disorders
citation.journal: Various pediatric psychiatry and psychopharmacology journals

sections.heading: Critical Safety Information
sections.highlight: Never stop clonidine suddenly. Abrupt discontinuation can cause dangerous rebound high blood pressure and withdrawal symptoms.
sections.black_box: There is no formal FDA black box warning for clonidine, but clinically, the major hazards are abrupt discontinuation and excessive lowering of blood pressure and heart rate. Both can be serious or life-threatening if not recognized.
other: Rebound hypertension: Stopping clonidine suddenly after regular use can cause a rapid, sometimes severe spike in blood pressure, headache, agitation, and other withdrawal symptoms.
Low blood pressure and slow heart rate: Clonidine can cause dizziness, fainting, and bradycardia, especially when combined with other blood pressure or heart medicines.
Sedation: Can significantly impair alertness, school/work performance, and driving, particularly when starting or increasing the dose.
Heart rhythm issues: Use caution in people with conduction abnormalities, sick sinus syndrome, or on other rate-slowing drugs (beta-blockers, some calcium channel blockers).
Kidney disease: The drug is partly cleared through the kidneys; effects may be stronger and longer lasting in significant kidney impairment.
Patch-specific reactions: Skin irritation, redness, and rash under transdermal patches are common and sometimes require switching forms.
Overdose risk in kids: Even a few tablets can be dangerous in a small child (excessive sleepiness, shallow breathing, low blood pressure). Store securely.
patient_counseling: Do not stop clonidine on your own. If you need to come off it, your prescriber will taper the dose slowly to prevent rebound high blood pressure.
Get up from sitting or lying slowly to avoid dizziness or fainting. If you feel lightheaded, sit or lie back down.
Check your blood pressure and pulse if your clinician recommends it, especially when doses change.
Report chest pain, very slow heart rate, passing out, or shortness of breath immediately.
Let every prescriber (cardiology, primary care, psychiatry) know you are on clonidine so they can adjust other blood pressure or heart medicines safely.
If your child takes clonidine, keep tablets and patches completely out of reach. A small overdose can be serious.

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Most common side effects are sedation, dizziness, dry mouth, and low blood pressure. In children, sleepiness, irritability, and behavior changes can also occur.
plain_language_list: Sleepiness or feeling “wiped out,” especially when starting or increasing the dose.
Dizziness or lightheadedness, especially when standing up.
Dry mouth and sometimes dry eyes.
Irritability, mood changes, or vivid dreams/nightmares in some people.
Skin irritation under the patch (if using the transdermal form).

common.incidence: Very common (up to ~30–40%+ depending on dose and form)
common.patient_note: You may feel calmer but also more tired, especially in the first 1–2 weeks or after dose increases. Nighttime dosing can help shift sedation into sleep. If you are too groggy during the day, talk with your prescriber about dose timing or adjustment.
Feeling lightheaded when standing up quickly is a typical sign. Stand up slowly, and drink enough fluids. If you pass out, have chest pain, or feel extremely weak, seek urgent care.
You may feel very thirsty or notice a sticky, dry mouth. Sugar-free gum, water, and saliva substitutes can help. If severe, your dose may need adjusting.
Some people describe feeling “slowed down” or having less physical energy. This can be helpful for severe hyperactivity but may be problematic if you already struggle with fatigue.
Although clonidine often improves sleep onset, some people have vivid dreams or nightmares. If sleep gets worse or nightmares increase, let your clinician know.

common.incidence: Common (redness or itching in many users of Catapres-TTS)
common.patient_note: Mild redness under the patch is common. If you notice severe itching, blistering, or generalized rash, contact your prescriber. Rotating sites and using a small amount of topical steroid spray before placement may help.

serious: Severe low blood pressure or fainting: chest pain, confusion, weakness, or loss of consciousness.
Symptomatic bradycardia: very slow heart rate, dizziness, near-fainting, or fainting.
Rebound hypertension and withdrawal symptoms if stopped abruptly: severe headache, agitation, rapid heartbeat, and very high blood pressure.
Heart rhythm problems in people with underlying conduction disease or on multiple rate-slowing medications.
Severe skin reactions to the patch: widespread rash, swelling, or signs of allergic reaction (swelling of lips, tongue, or face).
Depressed mood, unusual behavioral changes, or hallucinations (rare but reported).

sections.heading: Important Drug Interactions
sections.intro: Clonidine’s main risks in combination involve blood pressure, heart rate, and extra sedation.

items.with: Other blood pressure medications (ACE inhibitors, ARBs, diuretics, calcium channel blockers, vasodilators)
items.risk: Additive blood pressure lowering. May cause hypotension, dizziness, or fainting.
items.action: Monitor blood pressure closely when starting or changing doses. Adjust one or more medications as needed.

items.risk: Greater risk of slow heart rate and severe rebound hypertension if clonidine is stopped abruptly while the beta-blocker is still on board.
items.action: If both are used, and one must be stopped, usually the beta-blocker is tapered first, then clonidine is slowly reduced. Coordinate carefully with cardiology/primary care.

items.with: Other sedatives (benzodiazepines, sleep medications, opioids, some antihistamines, some antipsychotics)
items.risk: Additive sedation, confusion, and fall risk.
items.action: Use the lowest effective doses and avoid combining multiple sedating drugs when possible. No driving or operating machinery until you know how you respond.

items.risk: Combined use is common and usually safe, but careful monitoring is needed: blood pressure and heart rate may increase from stimulants and decrease from clonidine.
items.action: Monitor vitals regularly. Combination can be very effective for ADHD with tics, insomnia, or aggression when used thoughtfully.

items.risk: Additive sedation, dizziness, and impaired coordination.
items.action: Limit or avoid alcohol and THC, especially during dose titration. Discuss any substance use openly with your clinician.

items.risk: May reduce the antihypertensive effect of clonidine and increase risk of blood pressure fluctuations.
items.action: Monitor blood pressure carefully and adjust doses as needed.

sections.heading: Stopping Clonidine Safely
sections.text: Stopping clonidine too quickly can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure, along with agitation and physical discomfort. Tapering must be gradual and planned.
key_points: Never stop clonidine abruptly after more than a few days of regular use.
Typical taper in psychiatry: Reduce total daily dose by 10–25% every 3–7 days, depending on how long you’ve been on it and your dose.
For children on lower doses, prescribers often decrease by 0.05–0.1 mg/day every 3–7 days.
If you are also on a beta-blocker, that is usually tapered and discontinued a few days BEFORE clonidine is fully stopped, to reduce the risk of rebound hypertension.

Watch for withdrawal symptoms: headache, fast heart rate, sweating, anxiety, and rising blood pressure. If they occur, the taper may be slowed or a small dose reinstated and then reduced more gradually.

sections.heading: Dosing Information (Psychiatry-Focused)
sections.text: Dosing is highly individualized. Psychiatrists adjust clonidine based on age, weight, blood pressure, other medications, and target symptoms.

adult.adhd_off_label_initial: Immediate-release: 0.05–0.1 mg at bedtime, then add a morning dose after several days if tolerated.
adult.adhd_off_label_titration: Increase by 0.05–0.1 mg/day every 3–7 days, divided 2–3 times daily, watching blood pressure and sedation.
adult.adhd_off_label_typical: 0.1–0.3 mg/day in divided doses (some require up to 0.4 mg/day).
adult.ptsd_hyperarousal: Commonly 0.05–0.1 mg at bedtime, titrated up to 0.2–0.4 mg/day in divided doses, depending on response and tolerability.
adult.opioid_withdrawal: 0.1–0.2 mg every 6–8 hours as needed for withdrawal symptoms, with a typical max of 0.8–1.2 mg/day under medical supervision.
adult.insomnia_off_label: 0.05–0.2 mg at bedtime, often combined with ADHD or PTSD treatment; careful monitoring for morning grogginess and low blood pressure.
adult.hypertension_ir: 0.1 mg twice daily, titrated cautiously; psych prescribers usually coordinate hypertension dosing with primary care.
adult.elderly: Start 0.05–0.1 mg at bedtime, titrate slowly, and use lower maximum doses due to fall and confusion risk.
adult.hepatic: No formal adjustment, but start low and go slow; monitor for excessive sedation.
adult.renal: In significant kidney disease, start at lower doses and titrate more cautiously; effects may last longer and be stronger.

pediatric.adhd_er_initial: Kapvay/Onyda XR: 0.1 mg at bedtime for children ≥6 years.
pediatric.adhd_er_titration: Increase by 0.1 mg/day each week as tolerated; after first week, give as divided doses (morning and bedtime) for tablets; Onyda XR is usually once daily at bedtime.
pediatric.adhd_er_max: 0.4 mg/day (0.2 mg twice daily or 0.4 mg once daily depending on product).
pediatric.adhd_ir_off_label: Weight-based, typically starting at 0.05–0.1 mg at bedtime and increasing every few days. Maximum daily dose usually 0.2–0.4 mg/day depending on weight.
pediatric.insomnia_ndd: 25–50 mcg at bedtime (0.025–0.05 mg), increasing by 25 mcg every 1–2 weeks as needed and tolerated, within weight-based limits.
pediatric.tourette_tics: Often 0.025–0.05 mg/day initially, titrated in small increments to 0.1–0.4 mg/day divided 2–4 times daily.

sections.simple_explanation: For kids and teens, clonidine is usually started low at night and then slowly increased, sometimes adding a morning dose. Extended-release forms are better for all-day ADHD coverage. Immediate-release is often used for sleep, PTSD hyperarousal, or opioid withdrawal and may be taken multiple times per day.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, and Special Groups
sections.text: Clonidine can cross the placenta and into breast milk, and it affects blood pressure in both the pregnant person and fetus. In older adults, dizziness and falls are key concerns.
sections.pregnancy: Clonidine crosses the placenta, and umbilical cord levels are similar to maternal serum levels. It is not a first-choice medication for hypertension in pregnancy but may be used as an alternative when other options are not suitable and under specialist guidance. For ADHD or anxiety in pregnancy, other treatments (such as behavioral therapy or certain antidepressants) are generally preferred. If someone becomes pregnant while on clonidine, decisions about continuing or changing therapy should be made through shared decision-making with psychiatry, obstetrics, and possibly cardiology.
sections.lactation: Clonidine is excreted into breast milk, and measurable levels have been found in nursing infants. Some breastfed infants (especially those also exposed in utero) have shown drowsiness, poor feeding, hypotonia, or low blood sugar. When used during breastfeeding, infants should be monitored for sedation, feeding problems, and poor weight gain. Other options may be preferred for new starts, especially in preterm infants or when high maternal doses are required.
sections.pediatrics: Clonidine is widely used in child psychiatry but must be handled carefully. Blood pressure, pulse, and sedation should be monitored, particularly during dose changes. Kids can be more sensitive to blood pressure drops and behavioral side effects (irritability, mood changes, nightmares). Doses are weight-based and should be clearly written in mg or micrograms, not just ‘mL.’
sections.geriatrics: Older adults are more prone to dizziness, falls, confusion, and bradycardia. Clonidine is generally avoided as a blood pressure treatment in people ≥65 when other options exist. If needed for psychiatric reasons (eg, severe hyperarousal, withdrawal states), start at very low doses, monitor closely, and reassess frequently.
sections.hepatic: No specific adjustment in mild liver disease, but because clonidine is hepatically metabolized, prescribers usually start low and titrate slowly. Monitor for excessive sedation or mental status changes.
sections.renal: Because clonidine is partly cleared unchanged by the kidneys, its effects last longer in advanced kidney disease. Doses should be lower and titration slower; blood pressure and heart rate must be monitored closely.

sections.heading: What Clinicians Monitor
items: Blood pressure: baseline and regularly, especially during dose changes or when combined with other antihypertensives.
Heart rate: watch for bradycardia (slow pulse), particularly if the patient is on beta-blockers or has cardiac disease.
Sedation and daytime functioning: school or work performance, driving safety, and falls in older adults.
ADHD/tic/PTSD symptoms: rating scales, sleep diaries, and feedback from families and teachers.
Mood and behavior: irritability, depression, paradoxical agitation, or nightmares.
Withdrawal or rebound symptoms: headache, agitation, tachycardia, or rising blood pressure if doses are missed or reduced too quickly.
Skin under transdermal patches: redness, blistering, or allergic reactions.
Kidney function: in patients with known renal disease or on higher doses.
Adherence: missed doses can lead to significant fluctuations in symptoms and blood pressure.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Multiple formulations allow clonidine to be tailored to different uses—short-acting tablets for flexible off-label psychiatric symptom control and extended-release options for ADHD.
items: Immediate-Release Tablets (generic): 0.1 mg, 0.2 mg, 0.3 mg – used for hypertension and off-label psychiatric indications (PTSD hyperarousal, insomnia, opioid withdrawal, tics).
Extended-Release Tablets (Kapvay and generics): 0.1 mg – FDA-approved for ADHD in children ≥6; generally dosed twice daily.
Extended-Release Oral Suspension (Onyda XR): 0.1 mg/mL – ADHD treatment in pediatric patients, useful when swallowing tablets is difficult.
Extended-Release 24-hour Tablets (Nexiclon XR and generics): 0.17 mg – used mainly for hypertension but sometimes used off-label for smoother coverage.

Transdermal Patch (Catapres-TTS and generics): 0.1, 0.2, 0.3 mg/24-hour systems – changed weekly; more often used for hypertension than psychiatric indications but can support adherence in complex cases.

Epidural Solution (Duraclon): 100 mcg/mL and 500 mcg/mL – specialized cancer pain management as continuous epidural infusion. This is NOT a psychiatric route and is reserved for severe pain under specialist care.

sections.heading: How Clonidine Works
sections.text: Clonidine stimulates alpha-2 receptors in the brainstem, which decreases the release of norepinephrine (a fight-or-flight chemical) from nerve endings. This reduces sympathetic nervous system activity—the system that speeds up heart rate, tightens blood vessels, and keeps the body in a high-alert state. In ADHD and PTSD, this "downshifts" an overactive nervous system, leading to less physical restlessness, agitation, and hyperarousal. In the spinal cord, clonidine can also reduce transmission of pain signals, which is why it is used epidurally for refractory cancer pain.

sections.heading: Where It Fits in Psychiatric Treatment
sections.text: Clonidine is a niche but valuable tool in psychiatry. It is not a first-line medication for depression or primary anxiety disorders, and it does not work like stimulants or SSRIs. Instead, it has specific strengths: calming hyperactive, over-aroused nervous systems, improving sleep, softening tics, and smoothing withdrawal states. For ADHD, it is a nonstimulant option and an important adjunct when tics, aggression, or insomnia complicate stimulant treatment. For PTSD, it may help with hyperarousal and sleep but is usually added on top of trauma-focused therapy and antidepressants rather than used alone.

seo.title: Clonidine (Kapvay, Catapres): ADHD, PTSD, Sleep, Dosing & Side Effects
seo.description: Psychiatry-focused guide to clonidine: how it calms ADHD hyperactivity, tics, PTSD hyperarousal, and sleep problems; dosing ranges; side effects (sedation, blood pressure changes); and safe tapering.

editorial.reviewStatement: Content medically reviewed and aligned with current FDA labeling, pediatric ADHD guidelines, and major psychiatric pharmacotherapy references, with specific emphasis on safe use in ADHD, PTSD-related hyperarousal, neurodevelopmental insomnia, and withdrawal states.

faqs.q: What is clonidine used for in psychiatry?
faqs.a: In mental health, clonidine is most commonly used for ADHD (especially in children), tics/Tourette syndrome, sleep problems associated with ADHD or neurodevelopmental disorders, PTSD-related hyperarousal, and to help manage physical symptoms during opioid withdrawal. It was originally a blood pressure medication, so all psychiatric uses still come with blood pressure and heart rate effects.

No. Clonidine is not a stimulant. It is an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that calms the nervous system rather than speeding it up. It can make people feel calmer and sleepier. For ADHD, it is often combined with a stimulant if attention is still a major issue.

faqs.q: How long does clonidine take to work for ADHD?
faqs.a: You may notice sedation and a calmer body within the first few days. For ADHD symptoms like hyperactivity and impulsivity, benefits typically emerge over 1–2 weeks at a stable extended-release dose. It is not an instant-on medication like some stimulants.

Yes. Clonidine is often used to help kids and teens with ADHD or neurodevelopmental disorders fall asleep more easily. It works by calming the nervous system and causing mild to moderate sedation. It is not a traditional “sleeping pill,” and dosing must still be monitored because of blood pressure and heart rate effects.

Clonidine is not strongly linked to weight gain. Some people may gain a little weight due to lower activity or improved appetite from better sleep, but it is not a major metabolic offender like some antipsychotics. If weight changes are significant, your clinician will reassess your regimen.

faqs.q: What are the most common side effects of clonidine?
faqs.a: The most common side effects are drowsiness, fatigue, dizziness (especially when standing up), dry mouth, and sometimes constipation. Skin irritation can occur with the patch. Most side effects are dose-related and may improve as your body adjusts or with dose timing changes.

faqs.q: Why can’t I stop clonidine suddenly?
faqs.a: Because clonidine suppresses your sympathetic nervous system, your body adapts over time. If you stop it suddenly, that brake is lifted quickly, which can cause a rebound surge in blood pressure and heart rate, along with headache, agitation, and feeling very unwell. To avoid this, your prescriber will slowly taper your dose over days to weeks.

Clonidine (extended-release) is FDA-approved for ADHD in children 6 and older, and immediate-release clonidine has long been used off-label in child psychiatry. It can be very helpful when used carefully and monitored closely. Regular checks of blood pressure, heart rate, sleep, and behavior are important.

faqs.q: Is clonidine addictive or a controlled substance?
faqs.a: Clonidine is not a controlled substance and is not considered addictive in the way opioids or benzodiazepines are. However, your body does adapt to it, so stopping suddenly can cause withdrawal-like symptoms (rebound high blood pressure and feeling physically unwell). That’s why tapering is still necessary.

faqs.q: Can I drink alcohol while taking clonidine?
faqs.a: Alcohol and clonidine both cause sedation and can lower blood pressure. Together they can make you very dizzy, drowsy, or increase your risk of falling. Most clinicians recommend limiting or avoiding alcohol, especially early in treatment or when doses are being adjusted.

faqs.q: What’s the difference between Kapvay and regular clonidine tablets?
faqs.a: Kapvay is an extended-release clonidine tablet designed for ADHD. It releases the medicine slowly over about 12–24 hours for smoother symptom control, usually with twice-daily dosing. Regular clonidine (immediate-release) kicks in faster and wears off sooner, often requiring multiple daily doses. They are not interchangeable milligram-for-milligram.

faqs.q: Can clonidine be used during pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Clonidine crosses the placenta and enters breast milk. It is not usually a first-choice psychiatric medication in pregnancy or while breastfeeding. In some cases—such as difficult-to-control hypertension or lack of safer alternatives—it may be continued under specialist care. If you are pregnant, planning pregnancy, or breastfeeding, discuss the risks and benefits with your prescriber before continuing or changing clonidine.
